- [ASSISTANT_SAID] A building inspector can act as an expert witness for cases involving building codes, regulations, and violations.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] An expert witness presents an Expert Witness Report after performing an inspection of the relevant site.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The report should ideally convince the opposition to settle out of court.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] An expert witness can be hired by a defendant, a plaintiff, or by the court.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Both expert witnesses should be objective and neutral regarding the case outcome.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] An expert witness should have established credentials, knowledge, skill, experience, training, and education in their field.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Typical qualifications for an expert witness include being a practitioner, instructor, or published author in their field.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Building inspectors can provide assessments and opinions on building regulations and violations.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Building inspectors are often called in cases involving potential building defects that may have led to injury.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Examples of building defects include a badly finished floor or a water leak leading to a ceiling collapse.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Defects can be patent (obvious) or latent (less obvious and may manifest over time).
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Latent construction defects can include poor foundations, inferior materials, and negligent construction.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] A building inspector must determine if a fixture complies with building regulations and prepare an Expert Witness Report.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The report typically begins with a hypothesis confirmed by relevant facts and observations.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Expert witnesses can help determine liability for damages and make recommendations for remedying defects.
